newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain vows more austerity to ensure euro spot.
newsitem.headline: Spain vows more austerity to ensure euro spot.

text.p: Spain has promised to deliver fiscal discipline into the next century in an attempt to improve its economic pedigree and ensure a place at the launch of Europe's common currency in 1999.
The public deficit and debt will fall sharply by 2000, while growth will run at three percent or above from 1997 to 2000, the government said in a statement on Sunday.

Under the plan, the deficit will fall to 1.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2000 from a projected 3.0 percent this year and from 4.4 percent in 1996. This would be far less than the prerequisite for joining the launch of the euro.

Public debt will fall to 65.3 percent of GDP in 2000 from 68.2 percent in 1997. This fulfils the requirement for joining economic and monetary union (EMU) of achieving a decline in debt, but falls short of the 60 percent reference value set by the Maastricht Treaty.
"We foresee a more moderate evolution with healthier, more sustained growth," the statement said.

"This new pattern of Spanish economic growth is the result of a context of greater macroeconomic stability, the ongoing flexibilisation of markets...and our monetary integration with countries of traditional monetary stability."

For the conservatives, who took over government last spring after 13 years of Socialist rule, this plan is designed partly to assuage doubts abroad about Spain's long-term devotion to fiscal austerity.
The government has repeatedly said it was confident that Spain would pass the test of economic fitness on 1997 data which will be used next year to select the nations that launch the euro.

It argues that Spain now meets three of the five criteria, given inflation of 2.5 percent, a peseta that has been stable for more than two years and moderate long-term interest rates. It has promised to meet the deficit and debt criteria also.
This huge improvement has brought Spain -- once considered an outside shot for the euro launch -- to economic respectability and to the threshhold of the launch team.
Despite this, the government has still apparently failed to persuade the most powerful European nations that it means business on cleaning up its economic ways.

Early this year, German Finance Secretary Juergen Stark said some countries did not have the track record to join the euro launch. Although he named no names, market participants believed he was targeting Italy, Spain and Portugal.
For financial markets, the plan was seen partly as the government's attempt to tackle this sceptical view.

"The market is distancing itself some from the stability plan, because it has a certain political slant so the market is taking it philosophically, without reflecting on it further," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
They said the projections appeared a bit optimistic and were voluntary.
"From the fiscal point of view they are promising a certain level of restriction and one has to ask whether it's sustainable," an economist said.
